newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco ruling arms FDA to the hilt -- trade journal.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco ruling arms FDA to the hilt -- trade journal.

text.p: If a cigarette is a medical device used in the delivery of a drug, as Friday's federal court ruling asserts, the government is free to implement a welter of restrictions on cigarette sales.

According to a report due out May 10 by Medical Device Approval Letter (MDAL), a trade publication that monitors U.S. Food and Drug Administration reviews of medical devices, the FDA's options include the most stringent of obstacles for the tobacco industry.
How about a pre-market approval process for Marlboros?

According to the MDAL report, which the journal said is based on interviews with "key FDA sources and private attorneys," the FDA's options include requiring cigarette makers to tabulate deaths and injuries associated with tobacco, opening plants to FDA inspectors, re-labeling cigarettes, scrapping certain brand names, and holding tobacco company executives criminally liable for submitting false data to the agency.

U.S. District Judge William Osteen's ruling Friday that the FDA has authority to regulate cigarettes as drug-delivery devices was the latest in a seemingly endless series of blows against the tobacco industry.
Osteen ruled against the FDA in one important aspect, however, stating that the agency did not have authority to regulate advertising of cigarettes.
According to the MDAL report, regulatory alternatives available to the FDA include:
* Make tobacco subject to a "monograph," meaning the FDA can prohibit certain ingredients in cigarettes, many of which are more harmful than nicotine.
* Require cigarettes be "prescription drugs or devices" that can only be dispensed by doctors.
* Require that tobacco be dispensed by pharmacists along with smoking-cessation drugs.
* Require tobacco firms to pay "user fees" to the FDA.
* Require certain cigarette brands to be renamed, "rendering them less sexy or glamorous."

MDAL said the FDA has required some drug and device product names to be revised because they were misleading. Some tobacco advertising also could be deemed "labeling," which FDA has asserted in the past.
* Mandate tobacco makers, doctors and hospitals report adverse experiences to FDA's MedWatch program.
* Declare any "new" tobacco products, including filters, investigational drugs or devices and hence subject to FDA-approved clinical testing.

MDAL editor Kenneth Reid, in a statement accompanying a press release highlighting parts of the upcoming article, said he doubted a pre-market approval process for cigarettes would ever materialize because it would serve essentially to take cigarettes off the market.
"Cigarette makers also could argue they should be grandfathered from further FDA regulation because cigarettes predate enactment of the Food, Drug & Cosmetic Act of 1938," Reid said.
He said Osteen's ruling could cause "legal Armageddon," adding, "About the only job protected from downsizing at Big Tobacco is that of staff attorney."

Ron Morrow, tobacco stocks analyst at Rodman & Renshaw, said tobacco-company stocks were not in much immediate peril because the appeal process that will surely result from Osteen's decision will be lengthy.

Asked if the full scope of the FDA's power, as entailed in the MDAL report, was fully comprehended by Wall Street, Morrow said, "A lot of it was talked about early on. But has it been fully digested? Probably not."

Morrow noted that former FDA Commissioner David Kessler said at the beginning of the FDA's fight to control tobacco that "as a medical device, he will bring nicotine levels down to zero over 10 years' time."
"That was the stated objective," Morrow said.

"Was it a mixed blessing?" Morrow mused about Osteen's decision. "Yes, because it left open a lot of issues. If it were really that ominous, you would have seen tobacco stocks sell off a lot more aggressively."
((--New York Equities Desk, 212.859.1725))
